extracted.intended_audience: Applicants seeking registration to practice before the USPTO; attorneys/agents subject to OED registration review
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedures used by the USPTO Office of Enrollment and Discipline (OED) and the USPTO Director to decide whether an applicant 'possesses good moral character and reputation' for registration to practice in patent cases, and the appellate/petition procedures related to such denials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory registration requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. § 2(b)(2)(A) — the USPTO 'may require [agents, attorneys, or other persons representing applicants or other parties before the USPTO] ... to show that they are of good moral character and reputation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the underlying statutory basis for denying or granting registration; applicants must satisfy the Office that they meet this statutory standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory standard: 37 C.F.R. § 11.7(a)(2)(i)
rubrics_metrics.description: No individual will be registered to practice before the Office unless he or she has established to the satisfaction of the OED Director that he or she 'possesses good moral character and reputation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The regulatory rule places the determination in the OED Director's discretion and identifies the specific regulatory test to apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'good moral character'
rubrics_metrics.description: Good moral character denotes 'an absence of proven conduct or acts which have been historically considered as manifestations of "moral turpitude."' (Konigsberg v. State Bar of California).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The OED/Director applies this legal meaning when evaluating past conduct; demonstrated acts historically considered moral turpitude are disqualifying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof on applicant
rubrics_metrics.description: Pursuant to the statute and regulation, the petitioner/applicant 'bears the burden of demonstrating good moral character and reputation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The applicant must produce satisfactory evidence; failure to meet that burden supports denial. Challenges to other agencies' procedures (e.g., OPM) do not shift this burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of responses to authorized inquiries (37 C.F.R. § 11.7(g))
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director considers, among other things, evidence presented by the applicant in answer to questions authorized by 37 C.F.R. § 11.7(g).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants' written and oral explanations to OED/authorized questions are material evidence; thorough, credible answers are necessary to satisfy the Director.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credibility and consistency of applicant's explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: The credibility of an applicant's responses and internal consistency are critical; inconsistent answers or failure to address significant aspects of evidence raise serious doubts about moral character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: conflicting statements about frequency/quality of contact with a third party, or shifting accounts about knowledge of documents, count against the applicant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of prior investigations and external agency findings as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: OED may consider results and evidence from other agencies' investigations (e.g., OPM), but is not bound to adopt their legal conclusions as collateral estoppel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Circumstantial or investigative evidence developed by other agencies can support OED findings; legal errors or admissibility arguments in those agencies are generally irrelevant to the administrative character determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show Cause requirement and applicant's opportunity to respond
rubrics_metrics.description: OED may issue a Show Cause Requirement (see 37 C.F.R. § 11.7(j)); the applicant must respond and the Director will consider that response before issuing a decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timely, complete responses to Show Cause letters are necessary; the Director's final decision will weigh the response (or its insufficiency) heavily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative admissibility of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence presented to which the applicant is responding (including investigative reports and applicant responses) is admissible in the administrative OED proceeding even if not necessarily admissible in court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants cannot prevail by arguing that certain investigation materials would be inadmissible in a judicial proceeding; administrative evidentiary standards differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural requirement for petitioning Director for review
rubrics_metrics.description: An individual dissatisfied with the final decision of the OED Director may petition the USPTO Director for review under 37 C.F.R. § 11.2(d); the petition must be filed within sixty days of the mailing date of the final decision and accompanied by the appropriate fee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitions filed after 60 days will be dismissed as untimely; fees must accompany the petition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative weight of mischaracterizations or misleading statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Mischaracterizing facts (for example, describing a settlement as 'permission to reapply') or otherwise misleading characterizations are treated as reflective on an applicant's moral character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterization and candor in describing past settlements, disciplinary proceedings, or investigations are material; misstatements may weigh against registration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance of relationships and interactions with third parties
rubrics_metrics.description: The nature, depth, and documented interactions with third parties (co-authors, references, website collaborators) are relevant to assessing involvement in wrongdoing and credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of longstanding professional/personal relationships (co-authorship, mutual references, joint website) undermines assertions that a person was merely an 'acquaintance' and is probative of possible complicity or knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for technical/forensic explanation when contesting documentary origins
rubrics_metrics.description: Assertions about how digital copies or altered documents could have been created (e.g., 'minimal knowledge of computers' suffices) are insufficient without technical explanation; unsupported conclusory statements fail to rebut investigative evidence about document forgery or copying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants should provide specific, plausible, and supported technical explanations or evidence when contesting the provenance of forensic or digital documentary evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: OED Director's delegated authority and public protection responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary responsibility for protection of the public from unqualified practitioners before the Office rests with the Director of the Office (OED Director), who has been delegated authority to determine satisfactory showing of good moral character and reputation (see 37 C.F.R. §§ 11.2(b)(3) and 11.7(a)(2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Director's determinations about character are entitled to deference within the administrative framework; the Director's role is to protect the public interest in practitioner qualifications.
